### Problem 1: Conditional independence and Bayesian networks

Consider the following graphical structures, corresponding to
(different) Bayesian networks. For which network does the statement
$A⊥B\ | \ C$ hold? For which does the statement $A ⊥ B$ hold? Prove your
answers by the laws of probability.

![](images/BN%20SMCP.png){fig-align="center"}

1a) $A⊥B\ | \ C$ holds for Network a, $A⊥B$ does not.

Network a is a common cause structure/fork. Here, the node C is a parent
to both A and B. The arrows go from C to A and C to B. In this
structure, information flows from C to the children. If the state of C
is known and conditioned upon, A and B become independent of each other
because the common cause explains both. $$P(A,B,C) = P(A|C)P(B|C)P(C)$$
which is substituted in the following
$$P(A,B|C) = \frac{P(A,B,C)}{P(C)} = \frac{P(A|C)P(B|C)P(C)}{P(C)} = P(A|C)P(B|C) \implies A⊥B\ | \ C$$
However, since C is not null ($\varnothing$), they are not marginally
independent, meaning $A\not⊥B$.

1b) $A⊥B\ | \ C$ does not hold, for network B. $A⊥B$ does.

Network b is a common effect structure/collider. Here, A and B are both
parents of C. Arrows point from A and B into C. In a collider, the
parents are marginally independent. They only become dependent if you
condition on the child C or one of its descendants. Since we are not
conditioning on C here, A and B remain independent.

$$P(A,B,C) = P(A)P(B)P(C|A,B)$$ which is substituted in the following
$$P(A,B|C) = \frac{P(A,B,C)}{P(C)} = \frac{P(A)P(B)P(C|A,B)}{P(C)} \not= P(A|C)P(B|C) \implies A\not⊥B\ | \ C$$
While
$$P(A,B) = \sum_{c}P(A,B,c) =\sum_{c}P(A)P(B)P(C|A,B) =P(A)P(B)\sum_{c}P(C|A,B) $$
$$ = P(A)P(B) \cdot 1  =P(A)P(B) \implies A⊥B$$

### Problem 2: Markov blanket

Consider the following graphical structure of a Bayesian network:

![](images/BN%20SMCP%202.png){fig-align="center"}

Determine the Markov blanket $MB(D)$ of a node D and show that the
conditional probability $P(D|A,B,C,E,F,G)$ is the same as $P(D|MB(D))$.

2\) The Markov Blanket (MB) of a node in a Bayesian Network consists of three specific groups of neighbors: parents, children, and other parents of its children
Parents of D: A, B
Children of D: C, G
Spouses of D: Child C: D and Child G: D, E
MB(D) = A, B, C, E, G
P(D | A, B, C, E, F, G) = P(D | MB(D))

$$P(D|A,B,C,E,F,G) = \frac{P(A,B,C,D,E,F,G)}{P(A,B,C,E,F,G)} = \frac{P(A,B,C,D,E,F,G)}{\sum_{d} P(A,B,C,d,E,F,G)} = $$
$$ = \frac{P(A)P(B)P(C|D)P(D|A,B)P(F)P(E|F)P(G|D,E)}{\sum_{d} P(A)P(B)P(C|d)P(d|A,B)P(F)P(E|F)P(G|d,E)}$$

Since the bottom sum is over d, terms not containing d can be factored
out.

$$ = \frac{P(A)P(B)P(F)P(E|F)P(C|D)P(D|A,B)P(G|D,E)}{P(A)P(B)P(F)P(E|F)\sum_{d} P(C|d)P(d|A,B)P(G|d,E)} = \frac{P(C|D)P(D|A,B)P(G|D,E)}{\sum_{d} P(C|d)P(d|A,B)P(G|d,E)}$$

the terms left (A, B, C, E and G) are the members of the Markov blanket
of D, there is no F. D is conditionally independent of F, given the
Markov blanket. So...

$$P(D|A,B,C,E,F,G) = P(D|A,B,C,E,G)=P(D|MB(D))$$

### Problem 3: Learning Bayesian networks from protein data

In this exercise, we will use the R package BiDAG to learn Bayesian
networks from protein data. Download the data here. The data consists of
the measurements of 11 phosphorylated proteins and phospholipids derived
from primary immune system cells, subjected to both general and specific
molecular interventions. (Hint: read the help files of the package and
use default parameters unless otherwise stated.)

(a) First, run set.seed(42) for reproducibility. Read in the data in R.
    Report the number of variables n and the number of observations N.
    Visualize the data in a pair plot using the ggpairs function in the
    R package GGally. Randomly split the data into 80% training data and
    20% test data. Initialize the parameters using the function
    BiDAG::scoreparameters with the training data and the Bayesian
    Gaussian equivalent (BGe) score. \[Note: The BGe score is a
    fully-decomposable marginal likelihood function P(D | G) for
    scoring Bayesian networks. The main underlying assumption is that
    the data is normally distributed with N (µ, W^-1). The precision
    matrix W follows a Wishart prior W_n(T^-1, a_w), where a_w \> n - 1 is
    the degrees of freedom and T is the positive definite parametric
    matrix. The mean vector µ follows a normal prior N (v, Wa_µ) with
    a_µ \> 0.\]

Run install.packages("BiDAG") in the R console. Then load the package by
running library(BiDAG). You may need to install the missing packages
graph, RBGL, and Rgraphviz from Bioconductor.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 16
#| fig-height: 14
#| out-width: "100%"
#| message: false


set.seed(42)
data <- read.csv("2005_sachs_2_cd3cd28icam2_log_std.csv")
n <- ncol(data)
N <- nrow(data)
cat("Number of variables (n):", n, "\n")
cat("Number of observations (N):", N, "\n")

suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(GGally))

ggpairs(data)

```

```{r}
train_indices <- sample(seq_len(N), size = floor(0.8 * N))
train_data <- data[train_indices, ]
test_data <- data[-train_indices, ]

suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(BiDAG))
myScore <- scoreparameters(scoretype = "bge", data = train_data)
print(myScore)
```

(b) Learn a Bayesian network using the BiDAG::iterativeMCMC function.
    Plot the directed acyclic graph (DAG). Evaluate the log BGe score of
    the test data against the estimated DAG using the function
    BiDAG::scoreagainstDAG.

```{r}
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(BiDAG))
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(Rgraphviz))
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(graph))

myDAG <- iterativeMCMC(myScore)

g <- as(myDAG$DAG, "graphNEL")
plot(g)

testScore <- scoreparameters(scoretype = "bge", data = test_data)

test_log_score <- sum(scoreagainstDAG(scorepar = testScore, incidence = myDAG$DAG))

cat("Log BGe score of test data against estimated DAG:", test_log_score, "\n")
```

(c) Assume you receive new data where only phosphorylated proteins are
    measured but the phospholipids, PIP2 and PIP3, are not. You would
    like to impute PIP2 and PIP3 from (a subset of) the other variables.
    According to the Bayesian Network you learned in (b), which subset
    should you choose and why?

    For PIP3 {Plcg} because PIP3 is only dependent on Plcg. For PIP2
    subset {Plcg, PIP3} because PIP2 is dependent on Plcg and PIP3.

    If only using observed variables: PIP3 from {Plcg}, PIP2 from {Plcg}

    If sequential imputation: first impute PIP3 from {Plcg}, then impute
    PIP2 from {Plcg, PIP3}.
